hero.title: Your AI Safety career starts here.
hero.body: AI Safety expertise has never been more important than today. SAIN provides the community, courses and resources to help students and professionals join the AI Safety field. We provide a clear path through education, community and practical projects, then connect strong contributors to the organisations, programmes and roles where they can take the next step.

meta.title: About
meta.description: Stichting Safe AI Netherlands develops the talent the Netherlands needs to address the risks of transformative AI. The talent pipeline, the foundation documents, and the people who run it.

mission: Develop the talent the Netherlands needs.
Address the risks of transformative AI.
Make a first real contribution possible.
hero.body: That is the mission of Stichting Safe AI Netherlands. Transformative AI could reshape the economy, science, and society on the scale of a major historical revolution; whether that goes well is not decided yet. We are a national talent pipeline: local chapters on shared infrastructure, from first contact through courses and the Project Hub, with a handoff into the wider field. This page shows that path, what we have written down, and the people who run it.

path.heading: The Netherlands has the talent. It lacked the path.
paragraphs: On the current trajectory, AI systems may soon do most economically and strategically important cognitive work, including AI research itself. The critical question is not only what AI will become, but whether enough people are ready to shape what happens next. Right now, far too few are working on that problem.

Nobody can name the exact timeline, and we will not pretend to. Readiness is not something the Netherlands has by default. It is something people build, while European institutions are staffing their AI safety functions in the next few years.

The Netherlands has world-class universities, ASML at the centre of the global semiconductor supply chain, proximity to Brussels, and emerging AI safety groups. What it lacked was a unified civil-society voice and a clear path from interest to capability to meaningful contribution. SAIN was created to close that gap. We develop the people; the field puts them to work.

pipeline.heading: Anyone can start. The path narrows as you grow.
paragraphs: The Funnel Diagram is the whole organisation. The wide end is a free course anyone can join, no technical background required. The narrow end is full-time work on AI safety, in policy, research, industry or civil society. Between them sit the community, the Project Hub, and fellowships. Progress through it is visible, to us and to the person making it, and SAIN’s job is to make each next step reachable, so that every step someone takes compounds into a more effective mission.

We are open about where our effort goes. SAIN builds the wide end: getting people in, teaching foundations, and scaffolding a first real contribution such as a supervised research project. At the narrow end we mainly connect and refer, with introductions and referral letters.

We designed the pipeline with many good endings. Someone who takes one course and returns to law, medicine or public administration carries that knowledge into their profession, and a society fluent in AI risk is an outcome we actively want.
pipeline.record: So far the pipeline has produced more than 100 course graduates across nine-plus cohorts, currently around 60 a year, and peer-reviewed research at NeurIPS and ICLR. The aim for mid-2027 is 250 or more graduates a year, reached by running the same standardised course in more cities.

documents.heading: The rules we hold ourselves to are public.
documents.body: SAIN is a Dutch foundation, a stichting, the standard nonprofit legal form. The foundation holds the brand, the legal entity and the finances, so a local chapter never has to build those from scratch; chapters run their own courses, events and communities. Every programme is free. Three documents define how the whole thing works, and anyone can read them.

hero.heading: SAIN runs on volunteers
hero.body: Every programme is free because people give a few hours a week to run it. This page is the work, what you get from it, and the way in.
hero.photoAlt: People working together at a table during a hackathon

work.heading: Six teams, three to ten hours a week
work.body: Amsterdam, Utrecht and Groningen each run the same teams. Leads carry a team and report to the chapter’s director; team members carry a slice of it. Most roles are three to five hours a week, leads six to ten.

education.name: Education
education.description: Run course cohorts and discussion groups. Facilitate weekly sessions, support participants, and keep quality high across iterations.

events.name: Events
events.description: Plan and deliver the chapter's calendar. Hackathons, expert talks, socials, and the logistics behind them.

communications.name: Communications
communications.description: Writing, design, photography, video and the website. Make the chapter's work visible and on-brand.

community.name: Community
community.description: Welcome new members, be the first point of contact, and help people find their way into deeper involvement.

outreach.name: Outreach
outreach.description: Be SAIN's face on campus. Tabling, flyers, and inviting students to upcoming events.

research.name: Research operations
research.description: Keep the Project Hub running day to day. Onboard researchers and supervisors, track projects, and unblock problems.

work.paidNote: SAIN also hires a small number of paid national staff when a role needs it. Those roles are listed with the open positions.

returns.heading: You leave with work you can point to
returns.body: Volunteer roles at SAIN carry real ownership early. Leads report straight to chapter directors, and team members run cohorts, events and channels that actually happen. You work alongside people across Utrecht, Groningen and Amsterdam who are moving into the field themselves, and many of the introductions that matter later start here.
items: Experience with real responsibility, not shadowing
A network across three chapter cities
A track record in the field: cohorts taught, events run, work published

courses.heading: Two free courses run in Amsterdam
courses.note: The courses are independently run by SAIN Amsterdam and are not affiliated with UvA or VU. The certificate of completion is awarded by SAIN Amsterdam, not BlueDot Impact.
technical: Curious where your technical skills could make the biggest difference for AI safety?

SAIN Amsterdam facilitates the <bluedot>BlueDot Impact</bluedot> <course>Technical AI Safety</course> course for people who want to help close the gap between how fast AI capabilities are advancing and how well we can make them safe. Over six weeks, you’ll diagnose why building safe AI is so technically hard, evaluate current safety techniques (what works, what doesn’t, and where the gaps are), and map how defences might break by building your own “kill chain”. You’ll leave with a fundable action plan for where your skills can make the biggest difference. SAIN Amsterdam supports ambitious students in finding their next steps in an AI safety career.
Technical understanding is ideal, but not a prerequisite. This is a foundational course, covering the foundations of technical AI safety.
governance: What would it take to govern technology that is advancing faster than the rules meant to guide it?

SAIN Amsterdam facilitates the <bluedot>BlueDot Impact</bluedot> <course>Frontier AI Governance</course> course, which helps you build the judgment to shape how frontier AI is governed. Over six weeks, you’ll assess the evidence, compare competing strategies, and test your ideas through practical exercises and group discussion, leaving with a concrete plan for how you can contribute. Because the course leans heavily on US and China perspectives, our facilitators are encouraged to also bring in European and Dutch materials. Whatever your background, Safe AI Netherlands is here to help you take your next step toward a career in AI safety.
No governance background needed. This is a foundational course that builds up the core ideas of AI governance step by step.

fundamentals.summary: AI Safety Fundamentals has run three times in Utrecht, reaching more than 100 participants: BSc and MSc students, researchers, engineers, and public-sector staff. Four weeks, one hour of reading and a one-hour lecture a week, at Utrecht University in the city centre. In week four you choose a technical path, a governance path, or both. You get a certificate for attending all sessions; no previous background is needed.

sessions.title: Introduction
sessions.detail: High-level overview of AI safety, why it matters now, capabilities and diffusion, types of risks, and solution strategies, technical and governance.

sessions.title: Types of risks and incidents
sessions.detail: Social harms, frontier risks, misuse, loss of control; real-world cases and how research lags behind deployment.

sessions.title: Why AI safety is difficult
sessions.detail: Industry incentives, funding gaps, expert disagreement, slow regulation against fast labs, geopolitical race dynamics.

sessions.title: Path specialisation
sessions.detail: The fourth week splits in two. Take one path, or both.

paths.title: Technical AI safety
paths.detail: Jailbreaking, the scalable oversight problem, RLHF and reward signals.

paths.title: Governance
paths.detail: Overview of the EU AI Act, accountability in AI systems, international actors in AI safety.

technical.summary: Technical AI Safety is a four-week, in-person course at SAIN Utrecht for people who can program and know the basics of AI. Knowing how transformers work is recommended. Each week covers one area of the field: the first two weeks focus on how AI safety evaluators test models, week three looks at safety in robots and other physical systems, and week four covers securing AI agents. The weekly assignments use material from ARENA, an established AI safety training programme, and especially strong solutions are sent to ARENA for review and may be added to their repository. A workshop every Saturday from 13:00 to 15:00 helps you complete them. After the course, we launch a research challenge where our mentors help you develop your own ideas. Each week has about one hour of reading, one to three hours of assignments and a 1.5-hour lecture.

sessions.title: Introduction to AI safety evaluations
sessions.detail: What evaluations are and why we need them, capability versus alignment evaluations, and how to design one: threat models, datasets and scoring.

sessions.title: Implementing and evaluating AI safety evaluations
sessions.detail: Running evaluations in practice with tools, understanding the common problems that make results unreliable, and how results are communicated to policymakers.

sessions.title: Embodied AI safety
sessions.detail: The safety risks of robots and other physical AI systems, safety filters, using vision-language models to spot unsafe actions, and measuring uncertainty.

sessions.title: Securing AI agents
sessions.detail: How agents are attacked through prompt injection and their tools, why model-level defences fail, secure design and AI Control, and how AI can also act as a defender.

governance.summary: AI Governance is a new four-week course at SAIN Utrecht, open to everyone, with no previous background needed. Most AI governance courses focus on the US and China. In this course, we also look at their visions and ambitions and at where middle powers like the EU fit in. We also dedicate an entire lecture to how Europe and the Netherlands are regulating AI. Throughout the course, we read and discuss primary sources, such as government strategies, laws, and documents from AI labs, giving you the tools to follow developments in AI regulation and geopolitics independently. Each week has about one to two hours of reading and a 1.5-hour lecture.

sessions.title: Introduction to AI governance and AI safety
sessions.detail: What AI governance is, how it differs from technical safety, why it matters now, and the main risks: misuse, loss of control, and concentration of power.

sessions.title: AI geopolitics
sessions.detail: The key actors (governments, labs, safety organisations, the UN), US and Chinese visions and ambitions, and where middle powers fit.

sessions.title: The tools of the policymaker
sessions.detail: Analysis of past incidents like the Hugging Face case, system cards, and future scenarios.

sessions.title: Governance in Europe and the Netherlands
sessions.detail: The EU AI Act and its gaps, the EU AI Office and the GPAI Code of Practice, the Dutch AI landscape.

courses.discussionGroups: Between cohorts, two discussion groups keep meeting: one on technical AI safety, currently a mechanistic interpretability reading group, and one on AI governance and policy.
courses.research: The chapter is building a research track: red-teaming language models, safety evaluation, interpretability, and agent behaviour. Its projects run through the Project Hub.

utrecht.teamBody: SAIN Utrecht is directed by Riccardo Campanella. The team is growing across four areas: education, events, communication, and research. The chapter's work is funded by BERI, with mentorship from Pathfinder.

evidence.heading: This already happened in Utrecht

evidence.contributed: Members of SAIN Utrecht contributed to this research.

technical: Curious to learn about the technical approaches to AI safety?

SAIN Groningen facilitates the <bluedot>BlueDot Impact</bluedot> <course>Technical AI Safety</course> course for people who want to learn about the open problems in technical AI safety and the techniques to address them. It takes six weeks, with about three hours of reading and a two-hour discussion session each week. The discussion sessions are guided by a facilitator, creating the perfect space to both discuss the material and connect with others who are eager to work on AI safety too.
governance: Curious to learn about the governance challenges around AI safety?

SAIN Groningen facilitates the <bluedot>BlueDot Impact</bluedot> <course>Frontier AI Governance</course> course, which helps you build the judgment to shape how frontier AI is governed. Since the BlueDot course mainly covers the US and China dynamic, we have extended the curriculum with hand-picked materials on tackling AI safety from the EU’s perspective. The course takes six weeks, with about three hours of reading and a two-hour discussion session each week. The discussion sessions are guided by a facilitator, creating the perfect space to both discuss the materials in detail and connect with others who are eager to work on AI safety too.
courses.discussionGroups: Two discussion groups meet through the year, each with at least one experienced mentor: technical AI alignment (scalable oversight, evaluation and red-teaming, preference learning, robustness, deployment risks) and AI governance and privacy (policies, regulations, accountability, transparency and fairness).

groningen.teamBody: SAIN Groningen is directed by Tarteel Mohamed, with work organised across four teams: education, events, communications, and research operations; a structure other chapters are adopting as they spin up. The chapter grew out of the AI Safety Initiative Groningen (AISIG), running since 2023.

evidence.heading: 30 events and counting
evidence.body: Since October 2023 the chapter has run 30 events: hackathons, course graduations, research talks, pub quizzes, and socials; first as AISIG and, since 30 April 2026, as SAIN Groningen. Members' research has been published at NeurIPS and ICLR workshops.

meta.title: Start a chapter in Eindhoven, Delft or The Hague
meta.description: SAIN is starting chapters in Eindhoven, Delft and The Hague. Each city gets a paid, part-time starting team of four: a Chapter Director and leads for education, events and communications.

hero.heading: Start SAIN in Eindhoven, Delft or The Hague.
hero.body: SAIN has chapters in Groningen, Amsterdam and Utrecht. This winter we are starting three more: Eindhoven, Delft and The Hague. Each city gets a starting team of four people: a Chapter Director, an Education Lead, an Events Lead and a Communications Lead. All four roles are paid and part-time.
hero.deadline: Soft deadline {deadline}. Applications are reviewed on a rolling basis, with priority to early applicants.

building.heading: You would be building a chapter, not joining one.
building.body: You would be the person building a SAIN chapter in your city, and you will be in charge of setting up everything. However, you’ll have support: a funded national organisation behind you, and a network of advisors, researchers and partner organisations who want nothing more than your chapter to succeed.

cities.heading: Three cities with the most potential.
cities.body: We have identified these three cities as the highest-potential ones for us to expand to. Here is, very briefly, why we think so.
cities.inTouch: We are already in touch with people working on AI safety in these cities. Where people have already been running things, we can build on top of that and be much more ambitious. Already running something there and not heard from us yet? <link>Please get in touch</link>, so we can work together instead of duplicating efforts.

incubation.heading: Six months from starting team to SAIN chapter.
paragraphs: New chapters start as incubating chapters. From mid-December 2026 to June 2027, the starting team will develop the chapter towards a few concrete milestones. Importantly, although this phase is part of the incubation, internally we’ll treat you as a SAIN chapter from the start.

We’re ambitious about this. In some of these cities, people already run AI safety courses, and we want to build on that and go much further: courses with dozens of participants, events that bring hundreds of new people into AI safety, a community of hundreds in every city, and people moving on into real projects.

The exact milestones for June 2027 we’ll set together with you in your first weeks; how you get there is up to you. We’ll work together to make sure you reach your fullest potential. In June 2027 we will do a final review of how things have gone. Chapters that get there become official SAIN chapters, and the director and lead roles stay paid part-time positions.

community.heading: This is what you would be starting.
community.body: Discussion groups, hackathons, talks, and the evenings after. In Groningen, Amsterdam and Utrecht, people meet friends and collaborators at SAIN, and often find their next step in AI safety. Apply now, and a year from now your city has a community like this, built by you.

offer.heading: You won’t be doing it alone.
offer.body: Everything the three existing chapters learned the hard way is written down, set up, and yours from day one.

roles.heading: Four roles in every city.
roles.body: Every starting team has the same four roles. Open one for the full description. You can apply for more than one, and the form asks which city you are based in.

apply.heading: One form, and a decision by mid-December.
apply.body: Applications are reviewed on a rolling basis, with priority to early applicants. The soft deadline is {deadline}.
apply.hearBackHeading: Everyone who applies hears back from us.
apply.hearBackBody: If you are not in the starting team, you are still the start of the chapter’s community! We will send you what you need to join SAIN’s online community, so you are among the first to hear about new activities and opportunities in your city.
apply.strongTeamHeading: We only start a chapter when the team is strong enough.
apply.strongTeamBody: If we do not have strong enough applications to start the incubation in a particular city, we will open a second round later on.
apply.aboutBody: Safe AI Netherlands (SAIN) is a Dutch non-profit developing the talent the Netherlands needs to address the risks of transformative AI. We build the national AI safety talent pipeline to get people from first contact to first real contribution. Then we connect them to the institutions and organisations that need them.
apply.visas: We do not sponsor visas. If you are in the Netherlands on a student residence permit, you can still apply.

close.body: Apply by {deadline}. We read applications every week, so applying early means hearing back early.

meta.title: Project hub
meta.description: The SAIN Project Hub matches you with an experienced supervisor, arranges compute, and takes a project from open question to published finding. Voluntary, remote-friendly, and open for applications at any time.

hero.heading: Make a first real contribution to AI Safety
hero.body: The SAIN Project Hub matches you with an experienced supervisor, arranges compute, and takes a project from open question to published finding. It is voluntary, remote-friendly, and open for applications at any time.
hero.illustrationLabel: A scatter of observations on a plot. Two researchers, one seated and one standing and pointing, fit a single line through it; the fitted line rises clear of the scatter in orange and runs onto a pinned printed page, whose figure repeats the same line.

projects.heading: Find a project, then join it
projects.body: Every project SAIN supervisors have on offer, kept up to date by the projects team. One application form covers all of them: name up to three projects in it, and the projects team will introduce you to the supervisors within a working week. A VU or UvA thesis counts towards a degree there, so it is for that university’s students; every other project is open to anyone with the right background.

eligibility.heading: You do not need a university post to do this work
eligibility.offer: SAIN’s offer is one line: bring your expertise to AI Safety, and the community, supervision, and support are here to take it further. The rest of this page is the mechanism behind that line: how a project is chosen, what support looks like week to week, and where the work ends up.
eligibility.openTo: The hub is open to anyone with sufficient background:
who: Students at Bachelor, Master, or PhD level
Researchers, and people working in industry
eligibility.remote: Remote participation works. Applications are rolling, so you can apply whenever you are ready, and for supervised projects you hear back within a working week.
eligibility.notAJob: One thing the hub is not: a job. SAIN does not pay stipends or salaries; participation is voluntary and educational. What SAIN does provide is supervision, compute, coordination, and, within reason, help with conference travel.

process.heading: From open question to published finding
process.body: Every project in the hub moves through the same three steps. The handbook spells each one out in full; this is the shape of it.
process.label: The three steps of a project

choose.title: Choose a project
choose.intro: There are three ways in, and all three are normal.

routes.body: Every project a SAIN supervisor has offered is listed at the top of this page. Find one that fits your background and register your interest; the projects team introduces you to the supervisor.
Some projects run without formal supervision. One person leads, usually whoever designed the project, and SAIN connects collaborators and supports the work.
Write a short proposal: the question, why it matters, how you would test it, and what you need. SAIN's Project Team reviews it, and can help you shape it if it is not fully formed yet.

choose.criteria: Not every valuable contribution is a research paper: the work can be technical, governance, policy, or conceptual. When choosing projects, the team looks at three things: relevance to the Netherlands and Europe, relevance to transformative AI, and whether it can succeed on a small budget. If you are unsure whether a topic counts as AI Safety, the default answer is yes, provided you can articulate a plausible pathway from the work to reducing risk from transformative AI.

support.title: Work with support
paragraphs: Fill in the application form and, for supervised projects, you hear back within a working week. If there is a fit, a supervisor is formally assigned and the project gets its own channel in the community.

Supervision is a working relationship, not a lecture. You drive the day-to-day work; your supervisor helps scope the project realistically, reviews experiments and drafts, and steps in when a direction stops being productive. Meetings run weekly or biweekly, and you agree your commitment per project up front, whether that is five to ten hours a week alongside a degree or something closer to full time.

Supervisors come from universities, industry, and government. In academia they are usually at PhD level or more senior; outside it, they have several years of senior experience in a relevant role. Compute is arranged per project at the start, and computationally inexpensive projects are encouraged. Remote participation works throughout.

publish.title: Publish your findings
paragraphs: A project is complete when its main question is adequately answered, including when the answer is negative, and the result is published in a presentable form: a paper, a policy brief, an evaluation or open-source tool, or a blog post on SAIN’s Substack or LessWrong. You get feedback on drafts, and SAIN may help with conference travel within reason.
That is not hypothetical. Work from this community has been accepted at workshops at NeurIPS and ICLR, which is where most first contributions in this field land.
publish.allPublicationsLabel: All publications from the SAIN community

supervisors.heading: The people you would work with
supervisors.body: Every supervisor keeps a public agenda of the projects they would like to supervise. Read it before you apply: the strongest expressions of interest respond to a question a supervisor has already posed.
supervisors.superviseBody: If you have substantial experience in a relevant field, usually PhD level or above in academia or several years in a senior role in industry or policy, and the work above looks like something you could guide, more supervisors means more projects. You do not need to be an AI Safety expert already. Supervision is remote-friendly, meetings run at a cadence you agree per project, and the Project Team handles the coordination around you. Fill in the supervisor form and we will follow up with next steps.

close.heading: Apply whenever you are ready
close.body: Applications are rolling, and for supervised projects you hear back within a working week. Fill in the application form, or email the projects team if you are not sure where you fit and we will help route you.
close.handbookNote: The full process, expectations, and norms are written down. <link>Read the Project Hub handbook</link>

handbook.heading: The SAIN Project Hub handbook
handbook.intro: How the Project Hub works, from first application to published output. It sets out what participants, supervisors, and the Project Team can expect from each other.
handbook.buildsOn: Builds on version 1.0 by Alexander Müller (Director), Thomas Brcic (Former SAIN Groningen Co-Director), and Ilija Lichkovski (Research Lead).

contents.purpose: What the Project Hub is for

shortVersion.label: The short version
items: Anyone with sufficient background can take part: Bachelor's, Master's, and PhD students, researchers, people working in industry, policy professionals, and people with no formal affiliation. Remote participation works.
Sign-ups are rolling. Apply at any time and someone from SAIN gets back to you within a working week; matching with supervisors happens in rounds.
Participation is voluntary and educational. SAIN does not pay stipends or salaries, but supports projects with compute, introductions, and, within reason, conference and travel costs.
One address for everything: {email}. Keep it in cc on any email about a project.

handbook.contentsHeading: Find the part that applies to you
handbook.contentsBody: The handbook follows the life of a project. Start where you are.

intro: SAIN (Safe AI Netherlands) exists to prepare the Netherlands for the risks of transformative AI: AI capable of changing the economy, science, society, or global security on the scale of a major historical revolution. Every year, hundreds of people take a SAIN course or come to one of our events. The Project Hub is where they, and anyone else with the right background, make their first real contribution, with a supervisor or a project team behind them.

This handbook applies to participants working on a Project Hub project, supervisors affiliated with SAIN, project leads and collaborators on open projects, and anyone outside SAIN who wants to understand how the hub runs. Participants can be students, researchers, people working in industry, policy professionals, or people without a formal affiliation; supervisors come from universities, industry, and government alike.
purpose.name: The Project Hub used to be called the Research Hub. We renamed it because a lot of valuable AI safety work is not a research paper. A policy brief for a ministry, an evaluation of a model in Dutch, an open-source tool, or a clear Dutch-language explainer can matter just as much. Academic research is still very welcome, and still at the heart of the hub.
purpose.criteriaTurn: Three things decide which projects we take on
purpose.criteriaIntro: We welcome any project that meaningfully contributes to AI safety, whether technical, governance, policy, or conceptual. When we decide which projects and supervisors to take on, we look at three things.
criteria: Relevance to the Netherlands, and to Europe or other middle powers. Many projects should be directly useful here: to Dutch policymakers, regulators, companies, or the Dutch public. General work, such as an interpretability project, is just as welcome, but local relevance helps a project stand out.
Relevance to transformative AI. The project should address risks from increasingly capable AI systems, whether those risks play out now or are plausible in the future.
Feasibility on a small budget. SAIN is largely volunteer-driven, so a project should not need large amounts of compute or money to succeed.
purpose.topicsTurn: Almost any topic counts, if it reduces risk from transformative AI
purpose.topicsIntro: If you are unsure whether a topic counts as AI safety, the default answer is yes, provided you can articulate a plausible pathway from your work to reducing risk from transformative AI. To make the scope concrete, the hub especially encourages work in the following areas, without being limited to them.

topics.title: Technical alignment and interpretability
items: Mechanistic interpretability
Representation learning and feature sparsity for safer control
Steering and controllability of LLMs and other foundation models
Adversarial robustness and red-teaming of models
Detection and mitigation of deceptive or misaligned behaviours
Scalable oversight, debate, constitutional AI, and related methods
Robustness of RL agents and multi-agent systems
Safety benchmarks and evaluation metrics, including evaluations in Dutch
Agent foundations
Neuroscience-inspired alignment

topics.title: Hardware, compute, and security
items: Compute governance and hardware-enabled verification mechanisms
Semiconductor supply chains, export controls, and their role in AI governance
Security of model weights and AI infrastructure

topics.title: Societal impacts, governance, and policy
items: AI governance, regulation, and standards, with emphasis on the EU and Dutch context
AI and democratic processes: misinformation, polarisation, information integrity
AI and labour: job displacement, economic and social impacts
Privacy, surveillance, and data protection in AI deployment
Risk assessment for high-stakes domains such as CBRN, cybersecurity, and critical infrastructure

topics.title: Meta and foundational topics
items: Research methodology and evaluation in AI safety
Benchmarking AI systems' persistence, persuasion, or autonomy
Forecasting and scenario analysis for transformative AI
Epistemics, information hazards, and responsible communication in AI safety
Dutch-language resources and education on AI safety

purpose.principlesTurn: Five principles hold on every project
principles: Intellectual honesty. Always communicate accurately what is known, unknown, and uncertain.
Proactively consider near-term and long-term harms, as well as dual-use concerns: ways the same work could both protect and cause harm. <s4>Section 4</s4> covers this in depth.
Maintain a supportive environment across disciplines, sectors, and seniority levels. There is zero room for harmful authority.
Feedback, critique, and review are essential tools, not personal attacks. When receiving feedback, remember it is aimed at the work. When giving it, attack the ideas, not the person.

Respect confidentiality. Many participants and supervisors work at a company, university, or ministry. Never ask someone to share information they are not allowed to share, and do not share such information yourself.
purpose.principlesNote: Be extra wary of these principles when deadlines approach. Everyone is fallible, and when compromising on a principle is the difference between publishing and not publishing, holding the principle matters more than the publication.

beforeYouApply.modesTurn: There are two ways to take part
beforeYouApply.modesIntro: The hub currently runs in two modes. Everything later in this handbook applies to both unless it says otherwise.

modes.name: Supervised project matching.
modes.body: Students, early-career researchers, and professionals apply for a guided project with mentorship from one of SAIN’s supervisors. Supervisors publish their agendas, the projects they would like to supervise, on our website, and we match them with suitable applicants (<s3>section 3</s3> explains how). SAIN provides logistical and, where possible, financial support, such as compute. Projects aim to become a published output: a paper, a policy brief, a tool, or something similar.

modes.name: Open collaboration.
modes.body: Not every project needs formal supervision. SAIN connects people directly and supports the work with compute, visibility, and introductions. To propose a project, submit it via the form on our website; to join one, say so in the same form or reach out to that project’s contact person. Nobody plays the supervisor role on these projects, but one person leads, usually whoever designed the project.

after: Professionals can also start an open project around a question they run into in their own work: a policy advisor who wants to know how a certain AI risk could be monitored, or an engineer who wants to build an evaluation tool. Just make sure the question is one you can share publicly (see confidentiality in <s4>section 4</s4>).
Not ready for a project yet? That is completely fine. If you mainly want to learn, say so in the form, and we will point you to one of SAIN’s courses or reading groups. Many participants start there.
beforeYouApply.eligibilityTurn: Anyone with sufficient background is eligible
eligibility: Both modes are open to anyone with sufficient background: Bachelor's, Master's, and PhD students, researchers, people working in industry, policy professionals, and people with no formal affiliation.

To supervise, you need substantial experience in a relevant field. In academia this usually means PhD level or above. Outside academia, several years of senior experience in a relevant role counts just as much, for instance as a machine learning or hardware engineer, a security specialist, or a policy advisor working on AI or digital policy. In exceptional cases this can differ.
Supervisors do not need to be AI safety experts already. Deep expertise in your own field and a genuine interest in AI safety are often exactly what a project needs.
beforeYouApply.signUpTurn: You can sign up at any time
signUp: Sign-ups are rolling. Apply whenever you are ready, and someone from SAIN gets back to you within a working week.
Matching with supervisors happens in rounds (<s3>section 3</s3>).

Applicants for supervised projects tell us about their background and experience, which supervisors or projects they are interested in (up to three), what they would like to work on, and how many hours per week they can realistically put in.

Supervisors only need to give us the basics: name, email, organisation, the projects they would like to supervise, and a short bio and picture for the website. No Discord account or long document is needed, though the Discord is the best way to get to know the community.
For starting an open collaboration, we appreciate a fully fleshed-out proposal before you contact us, but if necessary we can help shape it.
time: Time commitment matters most. In comparable programmes, the most common reason projects fail is that participants cannot put in the time they hoped to. When you apply, give the number of hours per week you are at least 80% sure you can keep up, also during exam periods, busy weeks at work, or holidays. A realistic 6 hours beats an optimistic 10.
Hours and meeting cadence are then agreed per project at the kick-off. Projects range from roughly 5 to 10 hours per week to near full-time.

gettingStarted.roundsTurn: Supervised projects are matched in rounds
gettingStarted.roundsIntro: This is how supervisors and participants are matched. We are working on automating parts of it, but the steps will stay roughly the same.
rounds: Supervisors sign up with their agenda: one or more projects they would like to supervise, the background they are looking for, and how many people they can take on. We turn this into a profile on our website and promote it through our chapters, courses, and network.
Applicants apply and select up to three supervisors or projects. If none of the agendas fit, describe what you would like to work on instead, and we will try to find a supervisor for it.

Every round has a deadline, which we publish on our website. After it, the Project Team does a light check of the applications (is the form complete, does the background fit the project?) and groups them per supervisor.

Within a week of the deadline, each supervisor receives the applicants who picked them, decides who they would like to talk to, and usually has a short call of 15 to 30 minutes with them before deciding.
Once both sides say yes, we send an introduction email, always with {email} in cc, and the project starts.
roundsNotes: Thesis students: university deadlines do not wait for our rounds. If you are looking for a thesis supervisor or an external thesis project, mention it when you apply, and where possible we handle your application outside the regular rounds.

No match this round? We tell you, and suggest next steps: the next round, an open collaboration, or a course to build up relevant skills. With your permission, your application stays in our system, so you do not need to fill everything in again.
Your data: we only share your application with the supervisors you selected or, if you ask us to find a match for you, with supervisors we think are a good fit.
gettingStarted.applicationTurn: Supervised matching begins with an application
gettingStarted.application: For supervised project matching, or to join an existing open collaboration, fill in the application form or email {email}.
gettingStarted.proposalTurn: Open collaborations begin with a project proposal
gettingStarted.proposalIntro: Before a project is approved as a Project Hub open collaboration, the project lead completes a project proposal. The full structure below is what we expect when the goal is a full paper and collaboration; for other outputs, drop what you think is unnecessary. A mechanistic interpretability tool, for example, does not need a title and abstract, and for a policy brief the policy question and intended audience matter more than hypotheses.
proposal: Research or policy questions, and hypotheses if applicable
Intended audience: who should read or use this, for example researchers, a ministry, a regulator, or developers
Safety and risk considerations: dual-use, misuse, and infohazards, meaning information that could cause harm if widely shared
Needed resources: potential datasets, compute estimates, and how many collaborators for how much time
gettingStarted.proposalReview: SAIN’s Project Team reviews the proposal and either approves it as a Project Hub project, with or without revisions, or declines it.
gettingStarted.onboarding: Every new participant gets a rough overview of current projects, groups, and supervisors, an explanation of this handbook and where it lives, and, if relevant, access to compute or other support. Join our Discord by filling in the onboarding form; the invite and the information above follow from there. Supervisors are very welcome on the Discord as well, but it is not required: email works just fine.
gettingStarted.matchedTurn: What happens once you are matched or approved
matched: You are brought into contact with the relevant people. For supervised matching, a supervisor is formally assigned, we send an introduction email, and a project channel is created in the Discord. For joining an existing open project, you are officially added to the project and its Discord channel. For a new open project, we add it to our website, add you to the Discord, and promote the project so others can join.

In a kick-off meeting, you agree the time commitment (for example 5 to 10 hours per week, or near full-time), the meeting cadence, and the intended output. We encourage communication through the Discord; other channels can be agreed if preferred.
The project is registered internally and kept up to date as it progresses.
Where applicable, the Project Team sets up a GitHub repository under the SAIN organisation and gives project members access.

during.rolesTurn: Participants drive the work; supervisors steer it
during.rolesIntro: The Project Hub is run by the Head of Projects, who works on it full-time and is responsible for it end to end, together with the Project Operations people in SAIN’s chapters, who know their local universities, companies, and organisations best. Together they form the Project Team. On open collaborations, the project lead runs the project and coordinates the team. Each role owes the others something concrete.

roles.title: Participants are expected to
items: Take primary responsibility for the day-to-day progress of the project.
Put in the hours they committed to, and tell their supervisor or project lead early if this changes.
Show up to supervisor meetings prepared, with a clear agenda, results, or specific questions.
Fill in the weekly check-in form.
Communicate early about blockers or personal constraints.
Follow SAIN’s core principles (<s1>section 1</s1>).

roles.title: Supervisors are expected to
items: Provide regular guidance and mentorship, and high-level project direction, stepping in where needed.
Help ensure the project is well-scoped and realistic.
Meet at the agreed frequency, usually weekly or biweekly, and show up prepared.
Give timely feedback on drafts and project directions.
Watch out for projects stuck in unproductive directions, and for participant wellbeing issues such as stress or burnout.
Raise concerns with the Head of Projects or the Project Team where appropriate.

roles.title: The Project Team is responsible for
items: Maintaining up-to-date documentation, including this handbook.
Recruiting supervisors and matching them with participants.
Onboarding new participants and supervisors.
Keeping track of Project Hub projects and outputs.
Acting as the contact point, via {email} or the <discord>Discord</discord>.

during.rhythmIntro: During a project, the standard pattern is the following, though your team or supervisor decides the details:
rhythm: Weekly or biweekly meetings: discuss recent progress and blockers, refine direction and scope, review experiments, results, and drafts.

Weekly or biweekly check-ins: a short form for participants and supervisors noting what was tried, progress, and next steps. It keeps everyone accountable and lets the Project Team see how projects are going, and step in where it can help.
Contact with the Project Team whenever necessary, via {email} or the Discord.
deadlines: Participants: fill in the <weekly>weekly check-in form</weekly> every Sunday.
Supervisors: fill in the <biweekly>bi-weekly check-in form</biweekly> every second Sunday.
communicate: Use the agreed channels, ideally the Discord, for project communication.
Keep {email} in cc in email threads about Project Hub projects.
Respond within a reasonable timeframe: 2 to 3 working days for non-urgent matters.
Meetings are the supervised participant's responsibility: have a simple agenda, start with a brief update since last time (the weekly check-in helps you keep track), and end with concrete next steps.
Be explicit about availability: travel, family time, exam periods, busy periods at work.
Default to kind, precise, and honest communication.
during.milestonesIntro: Each project should specify intermediate milestones. As an example, not a fixed rule:
milestones: Weeks 1 to 3: getting to know each other and the project, literature review.
Weeks 4 to 8: a first proof of concept, such as a first experiment or a first outline of the policy brief.
Weeks 8 to 10: internal discussion of the project, initial results, and what to improve.
Weeks 10 to 12: working on the weaknesses found, new results.
Weeks 12 to 14: writing up the final output and submitting it.
during.supportTurn: SAIN supports the work but does not pay for it
during.supportIntro: This applies mostly to technical projects.
support: SAIN does not provide stipends or salaries. Participation is voluntary and educational.
If funding for conference trips, workshop registrations, or travel is needed, we may be able to help within reason.
Once a project is specified, the Project Team strives to give it easy access to compute and other resources. How much compute SAIN can help with depends on the project and is agreed at the start.
We encourage computationally inexpensive projects wherever possible.
Where it helps the project, we introduce you to relevant people: researchers, people in industry, or policymakers who could use your work.
during.integrityTurn: Integrity, AI tools, confidentiality, and dual-use

integrity.title: Integrity
items: Cite sources properly, after making sure you know what they actually say, and avoid plagiarism.
Be honest about experimental results, limitations, and negative findings.
Keep enough documentation that others could roughly reproduce your work.

aiTools.title: Responsible use of AI tools
aiTools.intro: We are not against using AI tools such as LLMs for coding or writing. Where a participant has considered it carefully and it clearly helps, we encourage it. However:
items: Always check outputs carefully. Do not uncritically trust generated content.
Avoid feeding sensitive or confidential data into tools unless you are confident they handle data responsibly.
Where relevant, disclose your use of AI tools.

confidentiality.title: Confidentiality and conflicts of interest
confidentiality.intro: Many participants and supervisors combine a project with a job at a company, university, or government organisation. To keep this clean for everyone:
items: Never bring confidential information from your employer, or anyone else, into a project, and never ask others to. Projects should be based on information that can be shared publicly.

Check your employer's rules on side activities, intellectual property, and publications before you start. Civil servants, for instance, often need to report side activities, and people in industry are often bound by confidentiality and IP agreements.

Be transparent about potential conflicts of interest, for example when a project evaluates a product or policy of your own employer. Mention it to your supervisor and the Project Team, and in the final output where relevant.
Unless explicitly agreed otherwise with your employer, you take part in the Project Hub in a personal capacity.

dualUse.title: Dual-use and infohazards
dualUse.intro: Work on AI safety can have paradoxical effects: it can make AI systems, the AI ecosystem, or people inside it less safe. These effects can play out in complex ways that are impossible to fully foresee. At minimum, spend some time thinking about whether your work could significantly increase capabilities or misuse risk if widely shared.
items: If in doubt, discuss it with your supervisor and/or SAIN's Head of Projects before public dissemination.
Possible mitigations: redacting sensitive details, internal-only or restricted-access reports, or delaying publication until the risks are better understood.

during.wellbeingIntro: The Project Hub should be a place where personal wellbeing is taken seriously and support is there for anyone who needs it. AI safety work, like any research, can be intellectually and emotionally demanding, especially under the publish-or-perish pressure that is unfortunately far too common. Combining a project with a demanding job or study can add to that.
wellbeing: Be honest about workload and stress levels with your supervisor, and supervisors with their participants.
Take regular breaks and keep boundaries between work and rest.
Remember that what matters most is gaining a better understanding of AI safety, not whether one publishes.
Speak to the SAIN team if conflicts or issues arise.

publishing.completeTurn: A project is complete when the question is answered
complete: The main question has been adequately addressed, including negative or null results, and the work has been published somewhere in a presentable form.
If relevant, infohazard and dual-use considerations have been treated appropriately.
publishing.deliverablesTurn: Final deliverables can take several forms
publishing.deliverablesIntro: Each project specifies one or more final deliverables. For instance:
deliverables: A research paper at a conference, journal, or workshop.
A blog post on <substack>SAIN’s Substack</substack> and/or LessWrong.
A policy brief or consultation response, ideally shared with the people who can act on it, such as a ministry, a regulator, or a parliamentary committee.
An evaluation, benchmark, dataset, or open-source tool.
A Dutch-language explainer or educational resource.
A Bachelor's or Master's thesis, ideally followed by a shorter public write-up.
authorship: Authorship should reflect substantial intellectual and implementation contributions.
Author order is handled internally within the project team.
SAIN and the Project Hub should be acknowledged in publications.
SAIN may promote your work as enabled by the Project Hub.
If you have an employer, check whether they need to approve a publication, and whether your affiliation should, or should not, be mentioned.
after: Send the final output to {email} as a PDF, with a link if it is published elsewhere. We put the PDF on our website, so it stays available even if other links break.
Output and other relevant resources, such as data, code, notes, and drafts, are stored in <archive>SAIN’s project archive</archive>.

We share the result with the outside world, for instance in a post on SAIN's Substack and on social media, and update the Project Hub figures on our website. We always check the text with you before anything goes out.
Write a short note on what went well and what could have gone better, ideally shared with the SAIN community.
The project may be extended as a follow-up.

escalation.intro: We hope you never need this section, but it matters that the path is written down before anyone needs it.
when: A supervisor or participant relationship breaks down, for example through persistent unavailability or unresolved conflict.
There is suspected misconduct, such as data falsification, harassment including sexual harassment, or plagiarism.
There are serious concerns about whether the project's direction is still aligned with AI safety.
Project scope, expectations, or time commitments have become misaligned.
escalation.pathTurn: The path runs from direct to leadership
path: Participant and supervisor or project lead: try to resolve it directly first.
SAIN's Head of Projects, or anyone in the Project Team.
SAIN's Director, if the conflict involves the Head of Projects or the Project Team.
escalation.skip: If at any stage you feel unsafe, or face harassment you do not feel comfortable raising with the person involved, skip levels and contact SAIN leadership directly.
escalation.remediesIntro: Depending on the severity and nature of the issue, possible actions include:
remedies: Reassigning the supervisor or participant to another project.
Removal from the Project Hub, or from SAIN roles, in severe cases.
escalation.contact: For anything in this handbook, applications, project questions, concerns: {email}. It reaches the Head of Projects and the Project Team.

supervise.intro: Supervisor expectations are in <s4>section 4</s4>. The procedure for a supervised project is:
procedure: You sign up via the supervisor form, and we publish your agenda on our website.
After each round deadline, you receive the applicants who picked you, talk to the ones you are interested in, and let us know who you would like to work with (<s3>section 3</s3>).

Together with your team, you prepare a short project plan (a lighter version of the project proposal in <s3>section 3</s3> is fine) and send it, with the list of people on the project, to {email}. Include contact details, and each person’s Discord username and GitHub username where applicable, as a minimum.
If applicable, a repository is created in the SAIN GitHub organisation, and participants and supervisors get collaborator access.
Every Sunday, participants fill in the weekly check-in form; every second Sunday, the supervisor fills in the bi-weekly check-in form. Both forms are linked under Deadlines in <s4>section 4</s4>.
Keep {email} in cc on emails about the project, so we know what is going on and can help when needed.
supervise.interested: Interested in supervising through SAIN? You need substantial experience in a relevant field: usually PhD level or above in academia, or several years in a senior role in industry or policy. You do not need to be an AI safety expert already, and we welcome any discipline.

close.heading: The hub is open on a rolling basis.
close.body: Sign up whenever you are ready. Someone from SAIN gets back to you within a working week.
